When we were handling 2,800 horses in the rather hurried way in which they had to be handled last fall, if there was only one gray horse that sold for $60 which was finally turned into our pens, we probably did not do too badly. I would hope there were not more. The suggestion was made last night that somebody offered the horse for sale, I presume right in Lafleehe, because we did not have buyers anywhere else, and that one of our men said that he would not accept the horse. A veterinary goes with each one of our buying parties and examines all the horses before we buy them. I cannot conceive that a veterinary and an expert horse buyer, because that is what they were, w'ould look over a horse at LaFleche that was offered for sale-and the place where it would be offered for sale would be very close to the stockyards-and then would not recognize the horse very soon afterwards when he saw it in the stockyards. It is alwa3's conceivable, o,f course, that somebody might make a mistake. But it is hard for me, knowing horse buyers and veterinar-ies, to believe that in that short space of time a man would not know a horse he had been looking at a short time before. If he did not, I would say he was not a suitable man to be buying horses.
I do not want to dtetain the committee; I know what the objective is, but I have some remarks to make.
Are they on this particular point?
No, they are not.
Mr. Chairman-

Well, now, can I have this understood with the hon. member for Wood Mountain? He made his statement last night; I have made mine: could we leave the further discussion of this matter until we reach the "special" items?
I think it would expedite the business if we could complete the discussion now, and -when we get to the particular item I need say nothing further.

I should have objected last night to the matter being discussed at all at this time. There is an item under the estimates where we can discuss it. That was suggested by the hon. member himself when he rose. As I said a moment ago, I was not listening as carefully as I should have been to what he started to say, and I let it go through. I think we should stay within the rules and discuss this matter on the proper item when we come to it.

What item is that?
The "specials", at the bottom. The special war item appears in Hansard of September 28, and it will be discussed along with "specials" at the bottom. It can be found on page 552 of Hansard.
I believe the understanding was that anything which came under the minister's war estimates could be discyssed on the general item.
No; under "specials" or under the proper item within the civil estimates.

Under the minister's civil estimates there are no items comparable with some of the items under the war measures vote, and therefor'e I think the proper place to discuss them would be under the first item.
It was not the intention of the minister to make a statement at this time on our production requirements?
The hon. member to my hon. friend's left wants to make a general statement.

I can understand the desire of the hon. member for the Saskatchewan constituency of Wood Mountain to discuss the horse situation a little further. He gave some information which, I think, farmers in Ontario will appreciate, that one can sell horses out there for $60, S80, up to $130 and $150, as against about $30 here. I hope Saskatchewan will do well with their horses.
I could speak for a long time on agriculture. As you know, sir, I come from one of the rich agricultural communities of this province. In field crops and live stock we far exceed any other county in Ontario.

Oh, oh.

Well, we do. not want to have a war on our hands; I will say that we are one of the most highly productive districts, and I hope all hon. members will be satisfied.
I am a great peacemaker.
But what I am concerned about, and what I rose to address myself to, is the future of agriculture, with particular regard1 to the constant drift of young people from the farms.
I 'believe that is something which should engage the attention of every hon. member. Unless we can do something to make farm life more attractive, this country is indeed in for a very difficult time. I have great hopes, of course, that the introduction of electricity in the rural areas will make farm life more attractive, and that modern machinery will play its part; but something must be done if we are to make it attractive - to our young people to remain on the farms. In the county I have particularly in mind, the county of Grey, this drift to the larger urban centres has been going on, and the country is that much poorer.
I think we may still say that we are primarily an agricultural country, although we have made great strides industrially, and that we depend upon the prosperity of agriculture to maintain our living standards and our general prosperity. It therefore does seem to me that anything we can do to improve the lot of the farmer and increase the general prosperity of agriculture will react beneficially to the entire nation.
Yesterday, when the hon. member for Fort William was speaking about having been raised on a farm, I recalled that I myself had that experience, having been raised on a dairy farm, so that I can appreciate some of the things which the hon. member for Calgary West was speaking about. I know that farm life has been and even now is more or less a life of drudgery, and I am now trying to turn over in my mind this problem: when we have finally achieved industrial peace and arranged a forty or forty-four hour week for the industrial worker, who in the world is going to work on a farm, for there are very few farmers who can finish their work, particularly seasonal work, in any such limited number of hours?
These are the observations I have to make, and I want to set the example of being as brief as possible. In conclusion, however, I should like to make a reference to the statement of the hon. member for Calgary West that some people here speak of Ontario as being "the old milch cow." As an Ontarian, I assure hon. members from western Canada that that statement is not accepted literally

Supply-Agriculture
here. As a matter of fact, a prominent farmer around St. Thomas, who at one time occupied the office of premier of Ontario, used that term, but I believe that in the main it was resented, because we in Ontario have a high appreciation of our great western domain. We can think back to the time when we enjoyed a measure of prosperity with western people, and we hope indeed' that they will return to that era of prosperity which will mean so much to all of us in eastern Canada, and, as far as that is concerned, all Canada. Therefore I assure the hon. member for Calgary West that we do not consider that in any sense we have been under a disadvantage in respect of western Canada, that we have enjoyed many advantages from our association and will continue to do so. So long as they are prosperous we shall be prosperous.

During the war, assistance was given to the dairymen and the poultry farmers of Vancouver island by a. subsidy on the feed grains which were shipped from the prairie provinces. If this is the right place to raise the question I should like to ask whether the minister proposes to continue those subsidies or to render other assistance - to the dairymen and poultry farmers of Vancouver island? *

I think the general
answer to that would come under an answer to the statement which was asked for last night by the hon. member for Souris; and my hon. friend over here is on his feet.
This is the third time I have attempted to speak on the matter I brought up last night. In m3' concluding remarks I asked three questions which were quite specific and fairly simple.

I would ask, Mr. Chairman, that you rule that the discussion of the horse question be left until ,we come to the appropriate item. It has been discussed at some length now. If you rule otherwise, we shall of course go on with it, but I suggest that it be left for the time being.
The minister's suggestion is perfectly reasonable. I think the hon. member should leave the matter until the proper item is called.
I shall be prepared to discuss it at the right time.

Agriculture is so important that we should devote a little more time to general considerations before we go on to special items. I understand that at present about twenty-five per cent or a little better
of the population of Canada are engaged in agriculture and that is the greatest number in any one industry in the dominion. Therefore the question of agriculture is perhaps the most important one before this committee. We have probably wasted some time in the past few weeks, but in any discussion of this important item there will be no waste of time.
In my opinion there are two questions to be considered, the immediate agriculture policy and the long-range policy. The immediate problem seems to be a matter of production. After listening to the Prime Minister's statement on his return from overseas, I am sure that all hon. members were more or less shocked into the realization that the situation there is far more grave from the point of view of food than any of us had imagined up to that time.. We were taken aback to learn that hundreds of thousands of people are likely to starve to death in the European countries, and we also realize that it is up to Canada to a great extent to supply the food for the people of Europe since we are the granary of the world.
What is to be done to encourage greater production? From what has been going on in the last six months, or almost a year, we know that production in certain lines has been falling off instead of increasing. That is particularly so in the raising of hogs. It has been pointed out to the government many times during the present session that farmers are going out of hog production. The figures quoted yesterday show the extent to which that is true. When farmers begin to go out of the production of a certain line there must be a very good reason for it, because, whether in war time or in peace, the objective of every farmer is to produce to his fullest capacity. I believe that the reason farmers have been going out of hog production is that the price has not been satisfactory compared with prices of other products, and the government should encourage farmers by guaranteeing a price which would be sufficiently attractive to make the production of hogs pay.
May I call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to a recommendation made by the Alberta farmers' union. He no doubt has a copy of the circular sent out some time ago, in which it is proposed that a guaranteed parity price of S21 per hundred on rail at the main western points be established. That would be one way of actively encouraging greater production of hogs. Another recommendation is to encourage western farmers to raise coarse grain by paying the existing bonus to farmers who feed grain of their own raising to domestic animals. We understand
Supply-Agriculture

that up to this time the bonus paid has not worked out to the advantage of the farmer who feeds his own hogs with his own grain but more perhaps to the advantage of those who buy grain to feed hogs. I do not wish to refer to eastern farmers, because I desire to go on record as being of the opinion that the problems of farmers, whether east or west, are similar and that there should never be any reason for friction or antagonism.
Another recommendation that has been made, this time by the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, deals with the price of wheat. The attitude of this group is clear on the question of wheat, because we went into that very fully in the debate on the speech from the throne. However, I wish to put on Hansard a resolution that has been passed by the executive of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, which appears in a journal known as "U.F.C. Information", which all members have in their possession, because I believe that this resolution comes as close to the line we have taken as anything I have so far seen. It proves also that the representations that we in this group have been making have been put forward not on behalf of our party but on behalf of the people we represent. Here is the resolution:
Whereas Trade and Commerce Minister the Hon. J. A. MacKinnon, has announced the intention of the Canadian government to keep the selling price of Canadian wheat to importing buyers from soaring above $1.55 per bushel for the next five years, but has made no statement to guarantee that the sale price of wheat will not be allowed to drop below that price during the five-year period; and
Whereas we believe that in accordance with the present price of other goods, services and wage levels, $1.55 per bushel basis No. 1 northern at Canadian terminal elevator points constitutes a fair parity of price level for wheat:
Therefore we the executive of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan Section Limited, resolve the following wheat price policy:
1.	That for the crop year 1945-1946 the initial guaranteed payment on wheat shall remain as at present, and that a subsequent payment be made to conform with $1.55 per bushel basis No. 1 northern at Canadian terminal elevator points.
2.	That for the four crop years following the crop year 1945-1946 an initial payment equivalent to three-quarters of the basic $1.55 per bushel or other parity price be paid on delivery and subsequent payments be. made at appropriate times to conform with $1.55 or other adjusted price to conform with parity.
3.	That in the interest of national, provincial and agricultural social and economic stability a minimum basic selling price of $1.55 per bushel must be maintained during the five crop years commencing with the 1945-1946 crop year.
4.	That legislation in line with this wheat price policy be enacted at the present session of parliament.
fMr. Zaplitny.]
I do not know how much hoipe there is of that being done.
5.	That in the event of failure of government agents to hold the selling price of wheat at $1.55 per bushel minimum, the executive of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan Section Limited, will appeal to our members to take appropriate and effective action to protect their interests.
I will not hazard a guess as to what the appropriate action which is mentioned there would be, but I have placed that resolution on the record so that it will be clear that what we have been talking about in this group, so far as parity prices are concerned, is something which the farmers in the greatest wheat producing area of Canada have been discussing. So .much for the immediate policy.
The long-range policy is also important and perhaps in the long run the most important. I was interested in Listening to what the hon. member who preceded me said about the trend of young people away from the farms and into the cities. Being one of those who also grew up on a farm, and having spent the greater part of my life there, I realize that there are good and sufficient reasons why young people have not found it possible to stay on the farm. Perhaps the easiest way to illustrate the reason would be to place some figures on Hansard showing just what the agricultural situation has been for a number of years. I hold in my hand some figures- most of them come from the university of Saskatchewan-which show comparisons between the farm population of the different areas and the share of the national income the farmers received during those same years.
In 1921, the farm population was about 33 *per cent; in 1928 it was about 28 per cent; in 1931 it remained around 28 per cent. By 1941 it had fallen to 25 per cent, which shows a downward trend all the way. Righit beside those figures we can place the dhare of the national income received. I have not the figures for 1921. In 1926 the farmers of Canada received 26 per cent of the national income. In 1929 they received 22 per cent; in 1931 'they received 13-9 per cent and in 1941, 18-2 per cent. The committee will notice that in every case the farmer did not receive a fair share of the national income, which is a pretty fair reason why there has been that trend of young people leaving the farms and going to industry. There are other reasons.
We go farther aqd see what the situation is in regard to the ownership of land. We find that in 1901, taking all the farms of Canada, about 87 per cent were fully owned. By 1941 there were only 75-1 per cent fully owned. The rest were either tenants or part-owned,

Supply-Agriculture
or something of that nature. If we take it by provinces we find that in western Canada, where the greatest number of farmers live, in 1901 the percentage of farms fully owned in Manitoba was 88-9 per cent; by 1941 that had fallen to 66-1 per cent. In Alberta in 1901 the figure was 95-8 per cent fully owned; by 1941 that had fallen to 62-8 per cent. In Saskatchewan, which is perhaps an extreme case, 96-1 per cent .were fully owned in 1901; by 1941 that had fallen to 53 per cent.
There is another reason why young people have been drifting from the farms to the city. They have seen that it is very difficult, in some years almost impossible, to feel secure on the land. But to go on with the figures, we find that even the total capital value of farm property has been decreasing over the years. According to these figures, taken from the dominion bureau of statistics, in 1931 the total capitalization with land, buildings, implements and live stock, was $5,247,753,468. By 1941, which is ten years later, where one would expect it to be much higher, it had fallen to $4,222,441,473.
There again the committee will see that farm values even in capitalization, instead of going up as one would expect them to, with new buildings being put up and land being improved, have actually gone down. I shall refer to one more set of figures which I believe may be the most important of all, because it is a reflection of farm conditions. It is a set of figures taken from the Curtis report on housing and community planning, 1943, which shows what conveniences there were in the matter of such things as electricity, telephones, baths and so forth. I shall just quote the figures for all Canada; I shall not take the time to give the figures for the provinces separately. Right across Canada there were 79-9 per cent farm homes in Canada which did not have any electricity to help the farmers with their work. Seventy-one per cent of them had no telephones and 92-6 per cent had not baths or showers. Hon. members would almost think that we go without washing for a long time in this agricultural country. Then 91-9 per cent had to do without flush toilets. When conditions are such as I have enumerated is it small wonder that young people leave the farm? The tragic part of this is that it is often the people with the most ambition and intelligence, the, most go and grit, who refuse to live under such conditions. What we find is that some of the finest of the young people of Canada are leaving the land and going to the cities where they believe that they will be able to make greater use of their talents and abilities and fulfil their ambition more easily than on the land. The
only way I know of that this trend can be reversed or arrested is by making conditions on the farm such that they will be attractive enough for the young people to stay there. That means the raising of the guaranteed price for farm products to a point which will make it pay to stay on the land; the provision of legislation to make the farmer more secure on the land, and a more progressive policy in the matter of research.
I have here some information on research which I think will be of interest to the committee. May I first of all quote from the first report of the interim commission on food and agriculture. One of the sections is headed, "Research" and reads as follows:
One of the principal functions of the organization will be to promote research in the fields relating to its work as a means of meeting the needs and helping to solve the problems of the peoples of its member nations. Competence and
Fersistenee in the search for knowledge, and airness and courage in promoting its application, will establish a solid basis for recommendations and action.
It will be noted by the committee that the food commission evidently felt that research was one of its key or principal functions, as it states in its first report. We also find that there is an awakening of interest in the matter of science on the farm chemurgy. I hold in my hand a pamphlet published by the NorthWest Line Elevators association, which gives some interesting facts about the possibilities of chemurgy in connection with farm products. We have been accustomed to thinking of farming as an industry which provides the food of the country. It has, of course, other possibilities, and if we take a progressive policy in the matter of research I think we shall find that it has far greater hope than we ever dreamed of. Here is a statement which appears in this pamphlet which I referred to a moment ago. I would not vouch for the accuracy of the statement because it is only an estimate. Here is what they say:
Almost every day new uses are being found for farm products. The industrial chemist is the ally of the farmer. Men of science, looking into the future, see an industrial stomach which will consume more farm products than does the human stomach of to-day. The National Chem-urgie Council estimates that an additional 50,000,000 acres may be planted to industrial crops on this continent alone within the next ten years.
As I say, that is only an estimate. We have no way of knowing how close we can come, to that, but we are given to understand that th? industrial stomach, as they call it, will in the future be able to consume even more than the human stomach in the matter of farm products. In order to illustrate some of the uses that have already been discovered for

farm products in the matter of plastics and things of that kind, I refer the committee to a few pictures which appear in the same pamphlet. I am sure that hon. members either have this pamphlet or can get it very easily. On page 3 I find a picture of a group of young ladies, I believe numbering six. That is not what I want to draw attention to, however, but the fact that practically all the clothes these ladies are wearing in this picture have been made from products grown on the farm. Here is the caption to the picture.
Skim milk, bamboo and grass clothes the modern maiden. "Lanital" a new textile, half wool and half casein (a product of skim milk), along with bamboo and grass were used in making the clothes these girls are wearing. Nylon stockings, a product of coal, air and water, cover their limbs.
That is one illustration of how these products can be used. Then on page 9 I find a picture of twenty-three separate articles used in the construction of automobiles, all of which were made out of the soya bean, which has been used so much across the line. Farther along is a picture showing synthetic wool which has been made out of soya bean protein. So it goes, one page after another, illustrating what is being done already in the utilization of farm products for industrial purposes.
I believe the expenditures we have made each year so far in connection with research for agriculture have been pitifully small in comparison with the great returns that kind of research could bring to the farmers. We in Canada seem to be haunted by periods of shortage and surplus. At one time we are crying because we have too much of something, too much wheat or too much of something else. Then, before we know it, we are short of this and short of that. I believe that if we could use part of our farm production for industrial purposes it would serve as a sort of stabilizer for our surplus products, and in future might provide new industries for western Canada which would check the tendency of people to leave the land and drift to the cities of the east, which as I have pointed out already are congested and crowded at the present time.
Those are some of the thoughts I wish to leave with the minister and the committee. I do not want to go into any greater detail just now, and will leave anything else I have to say until we take up the individual items. I hope the minister will see his way clear to do one thing at least. That is, to increase the amount appropriated for research in order to give the young scientists of this country an opportunity to help the farmers.

I am not particularly fond of making speeches, especially in the House of Commons, but something happened last evening which inspires me to do so. If I had been given an opportunity of making my speech last night, probably it would have been just as brief as the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West. I find, however, that owing to the delay I have lost some of the inspiration I had at that time.
I was sitting over there listening to the hon. member for Melfort, the hon. member for Battle River and the hon. member for Wood Mountain, and I thought of the many weary hours I had sat in this house listening to western members talk about conditions in their own part of the country. I cannot recall a western member ever telling us anything about happy homes, or contentment, or men who had got along and achieved comparative riches. We hear nothing of that at all; nothing but gloom comes from the lips of the members who represent our western provinces.
Come on out and see us; we will show you how happy we can be.

Well, you know that sort of thing makes me sick, and I was pretty sick when the hon. member for Calgary West rose in his place. You get so tired of listening to people constantly grumbling, people who hive nothing to be thankful for in this fair land of ours. When the hon. member for Calgary West rose and shot a ray of sunlight from Alberta down into this House of Commons, immediately my gloom was dispersed and I thought here at last was something to be happy about, one western member who had a good thing to say about his own country.
He is a lawyer, not a farmer.

He was very cautious, and perhaps he understated the case when he went so far as to admit'that we are not all broke. I have memories of bygone years, when my relatives and neighbours who had gone west finally found themselves sufficiently wealthy to return home for a visit during the winter months. A common comment from those people was, "I would not take your whole set-up here, farm and everything else, if you gave it to me as a present, if I had to live on it." Some went even farther than that and- said, "I would not take your whole township as a present if I had to live in this country." I spoke to some of them about the cold, but the answer always was, "Oh, yes, it is cold, but you don't feel it." So that everything was beautiful and grand. *

Supply-Agriculture
In 1913 I went west, as far as Edmonton, and the memory which lingers with me most vividly is that about every second man you met was expecting to become a millionaire overnight by dabbling in real estate. Of course that bubble burst; it did not pan out so well for those speculators. Then I made a trip west in 1938; I thought if I was going to get any good from this pass I might as well see the western coast, so I took two and a half weeks off. Of course in that time you cannot do very much more than get impressions, going from here to the west coast and back; but while on that trip I can remember going out to a farm in southern Manitoba and looking at a field that would thresh thirty, thirty-five or forty bushels to the acre. The farmer told me that was the twentieth crop of wheat in succession on that piece of land. What has any person to grumble about if he has land like that? I remember travelling west from Winnipeg and looking at the beautiful homes, the meadows, the stacks of hay, the cattle in the pastures, the shelters around the homes and barns. I thought, "Well, if there is a God's country anywhere, this must be it." When I was in Regina I remember going through the country and being simply amazed at the broad acres with wonderful crops of wheat waving in the wind. Travelling west out of Regina on the train I remember that a stranger sitting beside me said, "Isn't it monotonous"? I replied that it was fascinating, mile after mile of beautiful fields of grain. It was true that you might go many miles without seeing a home, and then you might see a little shack perched up on a high piece of land. My conclusion was that it belonged to some man who came out in the spring, used his mechanized machinery to put in a crop, went home until harvest time and then returned to take off the harvest, someone who probably worked for a couple of months a year and spent the rest of the time retired somewhere in town; a land miner-not a home builder.
An hon. MEMBER; On 25-cent wheat?
Mr. WARREN; Well, if you get enough wheat at 25 cents a bushel you still have a lot of money. I thought that last night the hon. member for Melfort found it pretty difficult to find anything under present conditions which would justify him to stop whining. He did whine when he endeavoured to have the Minister of Agriculture give him a five-year guarantee that conditions would not be any worse in the next five years. Well, the hon. member is pretty anxious to whine, when he must go so far into the future to find something to whine about.
In my travels I got along as far as Ca'lgary, and I recall with pride the means of travel between Calgary and Edmonton. Those two points are served by two buses and two trains each day.
Three.

Probably it is three now; it was two then. I thought of all the oil in the Turner valley and of the coal in almost any hill.
Anyway, I went out to see some relatives at Lacombe. I think of the young men who went out to the Peace River district, and of one in particular who has become h comparatively wealthy man within a few years. He would go into our granaries in the east, and would say, "When I go into one of your granaries and see your oats, it just looks like chaff to me." The fertility and productivity of western soil is remarkable.
In the area surrounding Lacombe they have everything within easy reach: timber, wood, plenty of water, oil and coal in abundance. Yet we hear this grumbling from members coming from Alberta. I have never yet heard one of them say a word in praise of his native province. When I saw that area I said: "Well, this is the garden of Canada, and probably the richest	province in the
dominion."
May I ask a question?
Well, it is nearly six o'clock and I want to finish my speech.
When the hon. member referred to chaff, was he referring to his speech or to the granaries?

Well, I can tell the hon. member that I am somewhat boiled up about this matter, and the effect this sort of thing is going to have on the young people from the western provinces.
Let me give an example. I happened to bo on the train and to listen to some boys who were sitting across the aisle from me, and were engaged in conversation. Those boys were on their way home, for harvest leave. After listening to them for a while, I learned where they were from, and eventually got into conversation with them. I remember particularly one fine young man-

He must have been from the west.

Supply-Agriculture

Yes, he was from Saskatchewan. He told me about coming home on harvest leave in the previous year. He said that he had arrived' home late at night, got on the binder next morning and run that binder steadily for two weeks or it might have been for twenty-one days. One of his brothers was on another binder during the same time, and all the grain they cut belonged to one family, for the family alone were operating the farm. They had cattle and horses-they had everything. Well, if you got only ten cents a bushel for all that grain, you would still have a lot of money. But here is the part that got me-
Then you woke up.
We'began talking politics, and the name of Jimmie Gardiner was mentioned. Well, one might as well have mentioned the name of the greatest criminal in the world.
Were you looking for votes?

No; I was trying to get the impression held by these young men. Jimmie Gardiner?-"Oh, he does not do anything for the farmers." Well, I thought of the millions of dollars spent in digging water-holes, in building fences for pastures, and all those other operations which have taken place in western Canada. I began wondering whether in the opinion of these boys there was anything right. They seemed to think everything was wrong.
What is the cause of that? Is it because we have had so many men going through the west trying to capitalize on discontent, and if there is none, trying to create it? Is that why these young people in western Canada are growing up in the belief that nothing is right and everything wrong?
It is because they have good common sense; that is why.
Well, that remark would help them a lot. I said to these boys, "What is wrong with you fellows? Does every western man expect to get rich?"
On 10-cent wheat!

He said, "We all expect to get rich." "Well," I said, "there you are.
'Mr. Warren.]
That is the difference between a western and an eastern farmer."

That is the exclusive
right of the eastern farmer, eh?

I said, "We eastern farmers have no expectation or hope of ever getting rich. We believe that if in a lifetime a man can manage to own a small farm, one which you would scarcely regard as a decent pasture, and can own a home and farm buildings, raise a family and give .them something of a start in 'life, we have done a pretty good job for one lifetime." But these boys admitted that they wanted and expected to get rich.
They had ambition.

I am not so sure that that is ambition, because there are so many things which enter into riches. A person can be very poor, as far as possession of this world's goods is concerned, and yet indeed be very rich; on the other hand, one can have large sums of money and still be very very poor.
In the minute left before six o'clock I should like to quote from tthe address by General H. D. G. 'Crenar, delivered recently at Upper Canada college, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of to-day. These were his closing remarks:
One further thought I would like to leave with you. You will get your true happiness in the life that lies ahead of you in accomplishing some worthy thing in which you are definitely interested. It doesn't matter, in my opinion, what that activity is, or whether it's a "white collar" or a "shirt-sleeve" job-providing only that it is useful, and not harmful, to others, as well as bein^ interesting to yourself. Also, it is quite unimportant whether it brings a large financial return, or a modest one. The main satisfactions we get out of life are the mental and spiritual-not the financial. I am sure, also, that it is not the length of a man's life which is important but, instead what he accomplishes in the time at his disposal. It is that conviction which enables me to think quietly, aad with pride, of the 22,000 and more, officers and men of the First Canadian Army who now lie buried overseas. They died for the sake of humanity and a future, better civilization. There could be no greater contribution in any lifetime . .

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, October 19, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Muskoka-Ontario).

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this important debate has had a rather long adjournment and I feel that interest in it will suffer on that account, but I am very glad that we are to resume the debate and to have an opportunity to express our views with regard to some of the proposals made in the budget and the general proposals for the country.
This first peace-time budget reflects, I think with but few exceptions, the outstanding characteristics of the present administration. The budget I would say is cautious and in most respects non-committal. Unfortunately it fails to display those qualities of foresight and imagination so vital to the solution of our problems. It contained, too, at the beginning a very important tariff change, but public opinion since tlhe introduction of the budget has been brought into play and I am glad to see that that proposal has been withdrawn. I hope that the new regulation regarding diesel parts and engines will, .before long, meet a similar fate. ,
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) committed the recovery of the country and the prosperity of its citizens into the hands of so-called private enterprise. The government, now that the war is over, foreshadows its own removal from the national economic scene; that is, its direct removal from the national social and economic scene. It entrusts Canada to the activities of groups and individuals whose motive has always been profit rather than public need. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), who incidentally made such a witty speech on the budget, seems to have missed the whole point of what I have just said. He poked fun at those of us who believe that the motive of production must be the satisfying qf human need, not the making of private profit. That, may I add, is the vital difference between a cooperative society and a corporation, a difference which the royal commission on the taxation of cooperatives in its report, which 47696-162i
we shall discuss when we have had an opportunity of studying it more carefully, seems to fail to recognize.
No one objects to anyone who gives service to his fellows receiving a reward for the service that he renders. The trouble with the economic system which my hon. friend supports is that it often demands its rent, its interest and its profit for no service except that of owning the resources and machines by which society must live. Even the authority he quoted, or at best the one sentence he quoted from Professor Lindsay, confused the issue by comparing an assured salary with an uncertain profit, for profit is not what the individual receives from society as a reward for his services and to meet his legitimate living and other expenses in rendering that service, but what he demands merely as the toll which society must pay because he somehow is in possession of the resources and machines to which every man must-have access in order to live. In our capitalist system the ownership of great corporations and financial institutions is usually divorced from the managerial function.

speechtext:
I think everybody in
this house knows that I do not have to read my speech. I was going on to say that the managers themselves are responsible to self-perpetuating boards of directors, who in reality exercise very often no managerial functions. The interest of those directors is of course in the strengthening of .the corporation and in the paying of dividends, the rendering of public service often being incidental to the two aims which I have mentioned. Thus Benjamin Disraeli's dictum that the possession of property should be synonymous with the performance of duty is almost entirely disregarded in our present society, and, if I may say so, the Christian ethic that ownership rni^t be synonymous with stewardship is almost entirely absent from the society in which we live.
We are entering a crucial period of our national existence.. Let us be realistic. Let us dispel from our minds the idea that since the world is no longer convulsed by a military straggle we shall merely revert, with no effort, to normal and peaceful living. I think every-
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

one will agree that we are living in an age of unrest and transformation. We have left behind irrevocably, it seems to me, the world we knew only a few years ago. We are entering a new and complex age, an age full of hope and yet replete with great peril, because the world is in the throes of a revolutionary upheaval, a revolutionary upheaval the like of which mankind has never seen before. For us to maintain the status quo and to effect only minimum changes such as would satisfy powerful social and economic interests in our own land and elsewhere would cause bitterness and resultant social and economic chaos. ''Our task in this house, as in every democratic parliament everywhere in the world, is that of endeavouring to make fundamental changes in the interests of the common man as rapidly and with as little dislocation as possible; in other words, to plan for changes by consent rather than by revolutionary upheaval.
Both the budget and the spokesman for the official opposition show no disposition to undertake such a programme. This is an age of science and of technology. The vast scientific strides that we have made during the war * culminating in the development of atomic energy show the need more that ever, we believe, for democratic control of the nation's resources both natural and financial. Unless proper supervision is exercised of the delicate and complex interrelationship between industry and the public and between industry and science, anarchy and chaos may well result. This we believe involves national economic and social planning under the leadership-hot under the day-to-day direction but under the leadership-of the democratically elected representatives of the people. That belief is now widely shared throughout the British commonwealth of nations, as was indicated clearly the other afternoon when Prime Minister Attlee addressed both houses of parliament.
Inextricably linked with the manner in which we govern our country is the manner in which we govern our finances. Does our present financial structure, exist as a means of serving the nation, the primary needs of the nation, or does it exist mainly to serve the interests of a privileged few?
Certain aspects of the budget fill my mind with doubts as to the ultimate goal of the nation's fiscal policy at the present time. Let us look at. one proposal in the budget. The budget proposes a flat sixteen per cent decrease in the income tax. This measure has been greeted somewhat enthusiastically by certain elements in our country, but as far as the bulk of the population is concerned this amounts to practically no reduction at all. It does not give relief to the
[Mr. Coldwell.1
small income groups which predominate in our society, but it aids those who do not need it; that is, it aids them mainly. I refer to the high-income individuals and corporations. A worker, with a wife and one child, earning SI ,500 a year, with a sixteen per cent decrease will save just S8.80 a year, or S2.20 for the remainder of this year. If I take a very moderate income of an executive or an employer, we will say one making or earning $6,000 a year, the tax relief in that case will amount to $263.52. In other words, the tax relief is going to those who do not need it as badly as some others in our society. Now taxation, to be just and equitable, must be based proportionately on earning power; if must leave all individuals a sufficient amount of money to provide themselves with food, clothing, shelter, and, I would add, those amenities of life to which this scientific age should entitle them; and it must not afford more relief to the wrealthy than to the poor. It is not what you pay in taxes that counts, but what you have left after your taxes are paid. Then may I add this too, that a reduction in taxes will not benefit a man wffio loses his job.
In marked contrast to our government's policy is the policy recently announced by the Labour government of Great Britain. That government has raised the income tax exemption. Of course it was during the war lower than our exemption.

speechtext: And still is.

speechtext:
And still is. But as a matter of fact the British exemptions as they now stand are higher than they were immediately prior to the war. They go down still too low; I admit- that. But in this first budget they relieved two million taxpayers of income tax by raising the exemptions above the prewar level. In addition to raising the tax exemption level they introduced tax reduction on a proportional basis. The lowest groups received the highest percentage reduction; the higher the income, the smaller the reduction; and, indeed, on very high incomes the surtax was actually increased. The result is that the British government has made, in the wrords of Mr. Dalton, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, "a further advance toward greater equality." Our own government has unfortunately not adopted the same policy toward the citizens of our country.	[DOT]
I should now like to remind the house-[DOT] because these figures have been put on the record a number of times during the last few years-of some figures regarding the earnings of waje and salary earners in this country. They are from the last available statistical report, the figures gathered in the 1941

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
census. According to these figures-of course they were samplings of incomes in groups- 1*9 per cent only of our population earned over S3.000 a year; 83-9 per cent of our population earned less than SI.500 a year. I should like the house to bear this in mind. Almost eighty-four out of every 100 wage and salary earners in this country made less than SI,500 that year; and to maintain a family of five in health and self-respect, the cost of living bulletin issued by the welfare council of Toronto estimated that in the year 1942-a better year than 1941 as wages went-$1,757 60 would be necessary. Now let me add this, to be fair, that while not all of the eighty-four per cent are heads of families, it is certain that a fair proportion are, and hence a large section of Canadian workers are not living-or were not living then, and I believe it is still true-at a proper subsistence level. If farm income were broken down for the same year the picture, I believe, would be darker still.
In a country with almost unlimited potential wealth and natural resources, in Canada, our country, I submit that this is little short of a national disgrace. Our first consideration must be, I repeat, the well-being of our citizens. When a government offers little or no relief to the bulk of the struggling citizenry it is failing in its obligations. Just as income tax is based on, a graduated return according to income, so the present decrease should have been graduated. I submit, therefore, that the government should have raised the income tax exemption level. Individuals who are married or who have dependents should be exempt, we believe, from all income tax if they earn less than $2,000 a year. The same exemption should be made applicable to single people earning, we will say, less than $1,000 annually.
The taxes paid at the present time by the higher income groups, in spite of their complaints, still leave a good margin for decent living. They are not in any immediate need , of such consideration, and therefore should wait for reduction until those less fortunate have received substantial relief. The farmer, I have always thought, not particularly in this budget and at this time, has been unfairly penalized by our fiscal policy. I need not remind the house of the various difficulties which have beset the Canadian farmer over the past many years. His income has never been constant. It is highly uncertain, .and perhaps that is emphasized to those of us who come from the prairie provinces, where farm income fluctuates gravely from year to year or from a period of years to a period of years. It fluctuates with extremes of
weather and markets. I have always thought and I have often said that income tax for the farmer cannot be approached or computed on the same basis as for the city dweller. He cannot be asked in fairness to pay on the basis of a yearly tax return. Taxation for him should be based on an average of annual income received over a period, say of five years. In this manner he would be assessed by the government for an equitable tax based on his average earnings. The minister should not have delayed this measure of relief to the farmer until a future .budget is introduced. May - I express the hope that when a future budget is introduced we may get this averaging of the farmers income for taxation purposes.
From the low extreme of the earnings of farmer and worker I should like now to jump to another extreme. We have seen the inadequate budgetary treatment of low-income groups. What consideration do some of the giant concerns in our country, colossal in * financial wealth and control over the lives of the Canadian people, receive from the government? May I add that these are the big fleas that afflict the distressed body politic especially in normal times and in days of near or actual peace-time depression. As the report on international cartels and monopolies, placed on the table of the house' recently, indicates quite clearly, they reach into every home and take their toll from every person in this country, rich and poor alike. They take their toll when we buy matches; they take their toll when we buy electric light bulbs, radio tubes, aluminum pots and pans, aspirin, drugs, paints and a host of everyday necessities which they control.
Allow me to try to remove any misunderstanding from the minds of hon. members as to the extent to which big industrial concerns have suffered under the conditions which have existed during the last six years. Let us take as an example a company which has been in the forefront of the news recently because of its opposition to its employees in regard to unionization. I refer, of course, to the Ford Company of Canada. From 1939 to 1944 the assets of the Ford company increased from $68,698,491 to $95,964,268, an increase of over $27 million, or approximately forty per cent. And this, remember, was during the war years when so many hon. members affirmed the need for equality of sacrifice. It has added over $6 million in the same period to its earned surplus account, earned surpluses being profits held by the company after dividends have been paid; and the statutory rebate of twenty per cent on excess profits tax provided for in 1942 will mean, I am told, a refund of a

I know you were, and that is exactly why I made the pointed reference just now.
To continue, Mr. Speaker. Thus the relief given for the encouragement of small manufacturing and business is in complete accord with the policy of the party for which I speak. Similar consideration should be given those engaged in agriculture, fishing and related industries which perform an acceptable service to our people. During the war many small businesses suffered. That in the war-time economy was perhaps inevitable. 'In the war years heavy industries producing capital goods were required. Impetus was given to such products and industries as iron, steel, shipbuilding, armaments, aircraft and so on. Today the largest firms are having the largest lay-offs. Government failure, I should add, to plan adequately for reconversion to civilian consumer needs has already begun to reap its fearful harvest of unemployment and insecurity. Lack of government supervision has meant quite simply lack of needed work and production, which in the end will mean restricted consumption.
The speech of the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario wound up with an amendment which has little relationship to his pleas. Indeed, I wondered when he read the amendment whether he himself had really drafted it; it seemed so unrelated to the speech which he made. For example, nowhere did he make effective or constructive proposals to ensure either full employment or full production. True he spoke of the necessity of both. He spoke with approval of Mr. Dalton's assurance that the socialist government of Britain had a five-year plan for economic and social progress, but he reminded the house with equal approval that in 1920 the Tory chancellor of the exchequer in Great Britain set

_________ The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
a limit on desirable public expenditures, the absence of which we now know, began the sequence of events which led British industry and her people to the brink of disaster.
The amendment demands the elimination of extravagant government expenditure. The hon. member dealt ably and well with the disregard of economy in military expenditures, which is a by-product of war. But taken in conjunction with his approval of the British budget of 1920, and the record of his party in the past, the inadequacy of his reference to worth-while social and economic legislation and to such projects as family allowances, a national health programme and so on, seemed significant of the kind of thinking which lay behind the words of the amendment.
I commend very heartily and sincerely my hon. friend's complaint that no adequate relief has been granted to persons in the low-income brackets; but if we are to maintain full employment and adequate social services we cannot reduce levies on high incomes and wealthy corporations. The relief of the low-income groups releases that purchasing power which is essential for the achievement of social objectives. Thus our revenues must be obtained more, rather than less, from high-income groups and corporations. This, it seemed to me, my hon. friend failed to recognize or to mention. On ithe contrary, his speech did contain a plea for the wealthy and privileged groups of this country. Having said that, I want to say, if I have misjudged my hon. friend-

speechtext:
- I shall give him an opportunity to set the matter right, because I am going to move an amendment; for although we of the C.C.F. could vote for the words of the amendment, we cannot vote for what we believe to be the substance of the speech which introduced it or what lies behind the words of the amendment. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maolnnis):
That the amendment be amended by adding to paragraph (a) these words:
"which require the use of our national credit in terms of public need to make possible a large-scale investment programme, the public reconversion of war industries for peace-time needs, the public development of new industries, of scientific research and of our natural resources."
And to paragraph (b) the words:
"and that no programme has been outlined for the expansion of essential expenditures necessary to provide complete social security and adequate purchasing power for our people;"
And to paragraph (c) the words:
"but, on the contrary, substantial and unjustifiable relief has been granted to large corporations and to individuals in the high income brackets."
So that the amendment would then read: This house regrets:
(a)	that no effective plan has been proposed to ensure full production and employment which require the use of our national credit in terms of public need to make possible a large-scale investment programme, the public reconversion of war industries for peace-time needs, the public development of new industries, of scientific research and of our natural resources;
(b)	that no satisfactory policy has been advanced for the elimination of extravagant governmental expenditures and that no programme has been outlined for the expansion of essential expenditures necessary to provide complete social security and adequate, purchasing power for our people;
(c)	that no adequate provision has been made for the immediate relief of the people in the lower income brackets from excessive taxation but, on the contrary, substantial and unjustifiable relief has been granted to large corporations and to individuals in the high-income brackets.
In other words, we have taken the amendment and added' words which imply policy to meet the objections made by the mover of the amendment. I am sorry to see the government place so little importance upon public works projects. With so much to be done in our country, with so many schools, community centres and hospitals, and roads to be built, with so much employment to be derived from such useful projects, I think it is unfortunate that so little emphasis is placed on such vital projects. It is not good enough to wait for a dominion-provincial agreement before going into such policies.
The wealth of this nation cannot be measured by the dry ahd lifeless statistics of a fiscal .policy. In the final analysis it can be measured, only by the amount of goods and services provided to its citizens, by the standard of living they enjoy, by their freedom from oppressive fears of want, war and illness.
In Canada, as elsewhere, we must increase our consumer goods. This can be done only if we are given the public investments necessary to develop our resources to provide essential services and facilities for distributing th'e purchasing power among the masses of the people, which is the result, incidentally, of a high level of employment. Key industries must produce, at minimum cost price, the equipment and materials the consumer industries need. But these basic industries, dominated by one or a few large corporations, have tended in the past to restrict output in order to maintain high prices. The cartel report placed before the house substantiates this fact. This has
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

been the hallmark of monopoly practice all over the world.. In this country, the production of such commodities as aluminum-and I may say something about aluminum later on when we are able to look into the report which was placed before the house-nickel, chemicals, and farm machinery is centred in the hands of a few major concerns. And, as I want to emphasize again, the truth of this statement can be found in the report tabled in the house a few days ago.
One result, among many of course, is that the small business cannot expand or flourish. To develop our natural resources properly, a public investment programme, plus certain phases of public enterprise, is the only lasting answer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, although there were some other matters with which I intended to deal to-night, I see that I am within two minutes or so of my time, and I do not believe in asking an extension of time when that is not in order. However, I wish to say one other word. I believe that the future prosperity of this country depends in a large degree on the encouragement of scientific investigation and development of our own resources. I want once more to make a plea for a matter which has been up in this house from time to time and which has been borne in upon me again over this last week-end, when I had an opportunity once again of meeting some young and middle-aged Canadians in the great country to the south who left our country because they could not find the opportunities to go on with the technical and scientific work for which they qualified in this country. We cannot. expect a man who has spent years in training himself for a particular scientific work, and who obtains, we will say, his PhD. degree, to accept $2,100 a year. There was a time just before the war when some were ready to scoff at professors and men with Ph.D. degrees, but that time has passed. Largely they are the ones who gave us radar; they gave us the scientific developments and economic advice that helped us to win this war; they have given us the power to develop atomic energy. I want to say to the government that I was disappointed ini reading the war appropriations bill and the normal estimates to see that there had been an actual reduction in the amount allotted for scientific research. To my mind, if you take the total amount allotted it is so relatively insignificant in our national budget that this house should look very carefully into the matter and do what it can to see to it that we retain and maintain in our employ those brilliant young scientists whom we are in danger of losing.

I -want to make that plea, not in a partisan spirit but because I believe the future of this Country depends so largely on the scientific development of our natural resources that all should make every endeavour to see to it that our young scientists are encouraged to remain in this country and do the job for Canada and for the. Canadian people for which this country has so well equipped them.
