speechtext:
There is really no difference except that Mr. Speaker has placed before the house the resulting amendment which my hon. friend's amendment to the amendment would bring about.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, in a good many respects this is a peculiar budget debate. My mind goes back to 1938 when a similar situation arose in the province of Alberta when I was presenting the budget in the legislature at Edmonton. I just got my budget before the house when I was called to Ottawa to deal with seed grain advances by the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning. For a period of ten days I had to leave my budget before the house to be shot full of holes in my absence. However, I note that in this case the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) guarded against any such thing and saw to it that the debate did not continue until he got back. I think that is a very good thing.
I should like to remind the minister that I am in good company. I recall that the newspapers of the day in their caridatures and cartoons on the front pages showed the minister of finance of Alberta as a mother who had just placed her baby on the doorstep of a big house, suggesting perhaps the parliament, and then was sneaking away and leaving the baby to its fate. Under the whole picture was the caption. "He has no mother instincts." I presume that there are two of us who have no mother instincts with respect to these babes, the budgets.
However that may be, it is my impression that it is the dream of every minister of finance to build a perfect budget, just as it seems to be the dream of every person with criminal instincts to plan and execute the perfect crime. I hasten to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not suggest any connection between the two, although many people consider the greatest criminal in the country is the Minister of Finance. "Kill 'Ilsley" seems to be a common slogan in many quarters of Canada. I sometimes think the minister does not make his burden any easier to bear by his inertia and his standardized attitude toward the matter of financial improvement and progress. However that may be, the minister has my sympathy and I want him to know and feel that.
No sooner is his dream of the perfect budget taking shape than along comes something or somebody to take the whole edge off it. Either a war starts or a tragedy occurs within the nation which necessitates the expenditure of large sums of extra money, or somebody gets an idea which starts a raid on the treasury from a dozen different quarters.
I can see the minister can appreciate that because of his experience. The urge to spend is very strong in the departments of government and so the dream of the minister is shot. In the end the minister is forced to bring into the house such financial proposals which do not in any way reflect his idea of a good budget. Here again I do not suggest that there is any connection between that very short budget and the one that he has brought in.
Let me make just a statement about the treatment now given to the Minister of Finance as a rule in this house. It seems to me that the treatment the minister receives as a rule does not help him very much. He does have suggestions made to him from time to time, but the criticism is usually pretty destructive. It must be quite cold comfort to a tired, overworked and harassed Minister of Finance to have some of hon. members rush in to help him hoist from the backs of the public and from his own back the old man of the sea

that is, the dead-weight of taxes that were spoken of by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell)-only to find that they have prepared for him a bed of Procrustes, on which he is supposed to rest when the burden is lifted from his back.
If our budget criticisms are to be of any value to the government it seems to me that they must be more than demands for reduced expenditures. Surely it is only reasonable that the minister might expect from financial experts scientific recommendations in keeping
The Budget-Mr. Low

with the advanced time in which we live. The minister has a right to expect from his critics something more than blind and misguided loyalty to narrow, financial and economic notions that have been outmoded for many years.
It seems reasonable, too, that we on this side of the house, and in fact hon. members in all parts of the house, should expect from the minister the application to his problems of some of the progressive mental thought and practice much more in keeping with an age in which any but the mentally atrophied must know and realize and recognize that what is physically possible can be made financially possible.
While the minister was presenting his budget and I was following most carefully his admirable presentation of a fairly complicated set of financial proposals, now and again my mind slipped back to the many budgets and the many sleepless nights I spent in trying to build budgets, and particularly to build my perfect budget-because I had the same dream. The figures which I juggled in those days were puny when compared with the ones the minister juggles. But the principle underlying the two were certainly just the same.
Later, as I studied the document, and supporting schedules and budget papers, I was tempted to do just a little budgeting on my own-just to keep in practice you know, in case the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) decides to make the Minister of Finance the president of the international bank for reconstruction and development, and asks me to take his place to help the Prime Minister get this country on a twentieth century financial structure.
But seriously, Mr. Speaker, I was anxious, as a matter of fact to look beyond the present ' year, perhaps even beyond the next year, to a time when our war and our main rehabilitation expenditures will have been reduced to peace-time levels, and when we shall be once more on a purely peace-time economy. To do this I set up, using the government's own figures and proposals, what appears to me to be the minimum peace-time burden of fixed charges and variables in the budget which the people of Canada will have to meet out of their production during the years to come.
I should like to refer to a breakdown of the budget which grows in my mind. These are the fixed charges that I find in the present budget: family allowances of approximately $200 million. I do not mean of course to criticize these, because I find myself in substantial agreement with many of them. Then, interest on the debt, including service, which

of course I do not agree with, including annual amortization and bond discount, premiums and commissions, 8400 million. Then, subsidies to provinces, not including special compensation to provinces in lieu of income and corporation taxes, $14,500,000 in round figures. Then, old age pensions, $33,500,000; superannuation and retirement allowances, $3,100,000; unemployment insurance; that is, the federal government's contribution to the fund, and the cost of administration, $20 million; veterans affairs, for rehabilitation and treatment services, payments to and for dependents, including administration of the Veterans' Land Act, and statutory amounts, $74 million. This makes a total minimum for years to come of $745,100,000 of fixed charges.
This represents merely those charges which are fairly thoroughly fixed as to minimum, so long as the government continues to operate under the present system of debt and taxation, and so long as it continues to honour its present commitments. Every single item in that schedule is bound to grow, except pen haps the item of interest and debt service. And even that will continue to increase verjt rapidly unless the government takes some determined action along sounder lines than has ever before been followed in government financing in this country. I might have more to say about this at a later stage, if time permits.
Thus far I have set out only the fixed part of the financial picture for the immediate future. There has yet to be considered federal government financial commitments in case the proposals made to the provinces under the dominion-provincial conference are given effect to. The chief of these follows-and the figures I present are only the increases in the expenditures above those which I have already included in the fixed charge burden necessary to fulfil the commitments to the provinces.
The first of these is national old age pensions and assistance, including administration costs, of approximately $200 million; health insurance, in the early stages only, of $70 million; subsidies to provinces, an irreducible minimum-and I am using only a minimum- of $12 per capita of provincial population, 'based on the 1941 production figure of $8 billion, giving an amount of $124 million. Then comes the extension of unemployment insurance-and this is an estimate after studying the proposals before the dominion-provincial conference-amounting to $20 million. These would total $414 million. With this added to the burden of fixed charges already presented of $745,100,000, we have a grand total minimum of $1,159,100,000 for years to come in those two items.

The Budget-Mr. Low
We might also consider the variables in our peace-time budget. These consist of defence budget and ordinary government budget which would include provision for trade requirements. These two will doubtless run normally at about $800 million, unless of course we carve back drastically our expenditures for defence, and also tackle seriously the problem of reducing administration costs.
It is my opinion that there is much that can be done, particularly along the latter line. The position this group takes is this: Cut out all. waste; carry on a businesslike administration; quickly find out the position where economy, efficiency and strength, meet, and then stay on that ground.
I -would remind the minister that some heavy bureaucracies have grown up in the past, ten years in the administration of this country, and it will require determined action on the part of government to get rid of those bureaucracies. But might I suggest most earnestly right here that the government see to it that in cutting down these staffs to an efficient peace-time level the fathers and mothers who gave their all, who made such a noble sacrifice during the war, and who were temporary war workers, be the last to be dismissed.
Taking the complete picture of fixed charges and of a variable running normally to about $S00 million a year, we can foresee these minimum normal requirements of approximately $2 billion a year to meet the programmes that have been outlined by the government.
This figure does not include any provision whatsover for debt retirement, and it does not provide for repayment to the people of Canada of the refundable portion of the income and excess profits taxes amounting to $444,271,000. These two items will require considerable additional expenditure above the $2 billion minimum if we are ever to cut down our very heavy load of debt. I suggest that we must tackle this debt problem realistically and at the earliest possible time. We should start reducing our debt now and keep on reducing it until the people of the country are free from the burden of debt.
If we assume that the total national production of $10 billion is maintained, the government will have to tax from the people a straight 20 per cent of their incomes or they will have to continue deficit budgeting, in which case the debt will continue to rise year after year, and consequently a larger portion of the revenues will have to be devoted to paying interest. My advice to the government is that they get on a pay-as-you-go basis as quickly as possible and stay there. With
flexibility gone from the budget, and with their bridges burned behind them, the government must soon realize that they are between the upper and the nether millstones.
I also suggest that it will require some rather bold and determined action on their part to keep those millstones from grinding them and with them the country to dust. Twenty per cent of the national income is a very high tax rate indeed. I suggest that it is a double tithe. When you add to that burden the weight of provincial and municipal taxation the taxpayers of this country face a pretty gloomy future unless the government makes a new approach to public finance, and I suggest that there is such an approach.
I said a moment ago that the government had burned its bridges behind it. What I meant was that the government of the day had committed itself to a very large programme of social and other services, resulting in a burden of fixed charges in the budget of one and a quarter billion dollars, or twice the size of the whole of the largest pre-war budget. But having given its undertakings, of course the government must carry through or go down or lose face. It is not my purpose to criticize the programme at this stage. I merely' want to emphasize and point out these facts in our Canadian economy. The government must-find it essential to keep the national production high in Canada. That is the first and most fundamental requisite of a prosperous peace time. No programme such as has been mapped out could possibly be successful without keeping the national production high. There is evidence, to me at least, that the government realize this quite well, and I want to assure them that this group in the Social Credit movement in this house will do everything within our power to assist them in keeping the national production high. In fact, we of this group are demanding an expanding economy wherein full opportunity is provided for Canadians to enjoy a rising standard of living. It is within reason.^ I am sure, that this should be. Canadian^ have always been ready to make any sacrifices necessary to bring Canada through her emergencies and through, her times of stress. Our people have made tremendous sacrifices during the past six years, and it is only simple justice, I submit, that Canadians should be allowed to enjoy to the full the security which the abundant resources of this country can provide.
In their efforts to ensure that production is kept up in Canada I feel certain that the government will face certain difficulties. I want briefly to warn the government respecting two or three of those difficulties and to pass on to

The Budget-Mr. Low
it if I can some helpful suggestions in connection with them. I do not have any desire for destructive criticism but merely to make suggestions that might prove helpful. In the first place in the efforts of the government to maintain production, I am certain that imbalances are likely to appear and grow in our economy. I believe that ordinary observation to-day reveals a great deal of these aggravating conditions in Canada right now. I shall take time to refer briefly to only two.
Live stock production has dropped dangerously low on the prairies and especially in the Peace River area, and this on account of the fact that tihe relationship ,between grain prices and live stock returns has been allowed) to become such as to discourage the production of live stock. The farmer will not slave from sunup to sundown or from long before sunup to long after sundown day in and day out throughout the whole year unless he foresees a reasonable chance that he will lbe paid for his work. He did not (hesitate to do this in war when he felt that his sacrifices would contribute to victory over our enemy. Right here I want to say that in my opinion Canadian farmers did make a magnificent contribution to Canada's war effort. But now that the war is over, it should1 be kept in mind that there is no financial incentive whatever for the farmer to keep his nose to the grindstone throughout the year feeding and finishing live stock. He can make a good living from grain and can get enough meat for himself and family easily enough. He responded splendidly in war time to the appeal for increased meat production and other production. But now he is five years older and he is definitely tired. Most of our farmers were middle-aged men when war broke out and the younger ones either went or were taken into the army. The older men carried on during the war without adequate help and now they feel justified, since the conflict is over, in taking things a bit easier.
I suggest with all respect that the shortsighted policy of the government in guaranteeing a price on wheat for the next five years without arranging a comparable and similar policy for meat production has resulted in a very bad slump in live stock prices. Cattle are not selling well at rural auction sales throughout the west, and especially in the Peace River district, where there are practically no hogs whatever for sale. The older farmers will not go back into stock raising without material encouragement and certainly they will not induce the younger returning men to raise live stock. The government have been repeatedly warned of this situation, but thus far it Seems that they have refused to see

the facts. An individual whose judgment I respect wrote me from the Peace River country, and I should like to quote a paragraph or two from his letter by way of evidence of what I have said. He said:
I personally, through filling out gas applications for several hundred farmers each year, on which applications a complete statement of live stock holdings was shown, could see what was coming up. Up until a year ago every farmer in this district listed from twenty-five to two hundred pigs. This last spring only one reported two hundred and the average was between one and five. If we had a quota to fill for Europe any sane man should see that rationing is not. the answer. What we need is a policy to build up production again to adequate levels to meet our own needs and at the same time to meet the-needs of starving Europe. This could easily be done. People up here have possibly not been heard in the rationing discussion, but.I can tell you as a fact that they have no sympathy for it..
The people up in the same section of the country. I am told, are somewhat bitter about, sugar rationing, believing that no effort has been made to increase production in Canada where refineries have operated' up to only a. little more than, half their capacity. They believe that, there is a combine racket in this field; my judgment tells me that there is something very peculiar about the situation, and I aim to get to the bottom of it when I have time.
What I wanted to emphasize was that as we set out to bring up our national production to the level required, if the Canadian people are to meet the demands of the various governments for taxes and services, we must take pains to establish by every means possible a balanced economy. One of the essentials in this effort must be a price structure that is based upon the parity principle and that will guarantee primary producers in every field their fair share of the national income and the national production. It goes without saying, too, that if we are to be successful in our efforts in this respect there must be some vision on the part of the government and also close and sympathetic cooperation amongst the Department of Finance and the Departments of Agriculture and Trade and Commerce.
I turn to a second problem that will have to be faced. In the second place, as the programme of full production gets under way, the government must- be on its guard against the building up in Canada once more of huge unsaleable surpluses of goods. A careful study of economic experience of the past reveals, to me at any rate, that when unsaleable surpluses begin to show themselves in the country we are beginning to enter a depression period. What has been striking to me. ^r, is this. A study of depressions

The Budget-Mr. Low
shows that they recur at intervals largely in inverse proportion to the inability of the Canadian people to produce; that is to say, that the interval of years between major depressions grows shorter when our productive capacity increases, and roughly in the same proportion.
What does this mean? Let us take a glance at the facts of the history of the past fifteen years. I recall that when, on October 12. the minister presented his budget he indulged in some history. I propose to do a bit of the same thing.
In 1929 Canada ran into a period of business recession the like of which we had not had in our history before. Merchants at that time found themselves with full shelves and warehouses but with few customers able to buy the goods they had in abundance. Consequently merchants ordered no more goods from wholesalers; wholesalers, with full warehouses, cancelled orders from manufacturers; and manufacturers, unable to get orders, laid off men and therefore stopped paying wages to the men. This reduced still further the . ability of people generally to buy the goods which retailers had for sale; and worse still, it started the vicious circle which ended up in a first-class [DOT] unemployment problem. Bread lines, trade stagnation, and poverty in the midst of abundance became the order of that day,, and to make matters worse, during the first fifteen months after 1930 more than S900 million in purchasing power was withdrawn from circulation in Canada and was cancelled out of existence.
Did this condition of depression come about because producers would not produce? No; that is not true. Common observation at that time revealed that production remained fairly high in almost every branch of productive effort, until the country was surfeited with goods of almost every description that we could produce. Was it, then, because distributors would not distribute the goods? I submit that the almost frantic race for markets which drove prices down far below economic levels indicates that distributors did their best to sell their goods. We all remember that, in their efforts to remove the goods which lined their shelves, distributors resorted to deferred payment plans which mortgaged years of the future earnings of those still fortunate enough in this country to have work, and therefore incomes.
It was about this time we began to hear the old Fabian cry, "the poor are poor because the -rich are rich", and the idea carried with it was, of course, "soak the rich." Was that the explanation of the whole sordid condition which existed then? I maintain that
that contention is stupid when it is subjected to careful scrutiny. If it were true that the poor were poor because the rich were rich, then I submit that a steeply-graded income tax that bore heavily upon the rich, with the proceeds distributed among the poor, would have solved the whole problem. That is exactly what was tried, notably in England. The poor for a' while were a bit better off through the dole, but the process finally intensified the ills rather than cured them.
Social Crediters at that time said that the first sensible step to take in starting back toward prosperity would be for the government to lay down a financial policy under which purchasing power in considerable quantities could be put into the hands of the consumers of the country. If this had been done the goods on the shelves of merchants and other distributors throughout Canada would have begun to move out into the hands of consumers; retailers would have ordered from wholesalers; wholesalers would have placed orders with manufacturers who, to fill their orders, would have had to take on men to work in their factories. The salaries paid to those men would have stimulated business all the way along the line, and as a result Canada would have started along the road to recovery. Social Crediters advocated that policy in season and out of season. We pleaded with the minister of finance of that day, but he said that there was no money, and anyhow, he contended, such a procedure would cause a dangerous inflation. So that the situation was allowed to drift and to deteriorate until war broke out in 1939. The banks and other financial institutions in this country clung to the same hoary theory of inflation as was held by the then minister of finance. They stoutly claimed that there was no money to start the wheels turning to put men back to work. "Where is the money to come from?" was their frenzied cry. Social Crediters replied, "where all money comes from, the end of a fountain pen in the hands of those authorized by law to write the figures in the ledgers of the banks." Of course we were looked upon as crazy, but I have noticed that some other people have since caught a measure of the same kind of craziness.
The Minister of Finance, in reviewing on October 12 the principles which he laid down in his first war-time budget at the special session of 1939, said, as reported in Hansard, at page 1035:
The second principle enunciated in September, 1939, was, that after an initial credit expansion, designed to facilitate a rapid increase in production, we should -endeavour to limit our borrowings as closely as possible to the genuine savings of the country.
The Budget-Mr: Low

Now just a word about this principle; immediately upon the outbreak of war the government took the first important step toward making Canada ready for a strong war effort. As the Minister of Finance said, "they arranged an initial credit expansion to facilitate a rapid increase in production." In taking that step the government also initiated the process of making Canada once more a prosperous country, a thing she had not been since 1929. The government did not take long to make up its mind what had to b'e done in the emergency to enable us to fight a military war. I wonder why it did not occur to the government that a similar step might have proved just as effective in preparing Canada for a successful fight in the economic war that we had back in the thirties? No member of the cabinet would deny that a good fight against poverty is just as important as, and perhaps in some circumstances more important than, a strong military campaign. Anyhow, that first credit expansion was arranged. As a result of it, Canada quickly stepped up her production year by year, until by 1945 we were able to produce nearly three times the total value of what we produced in the last pre-war year. I do not know who finally convinced the Liberal government that the first step necessary in our programme of making ready for an effective war effort was to increase the amount of money in circulation in Canada. But I do know that for some years before the war we Social Crediters pleaded with the government to start things going by arranging an expansion of credits-to use, in fact, the social credit of this country. We were ridiculed, but our contentions, in some measure at least, have been vindicated by time and history. Just to emphasize how far we have gone down the road of "credit expansion", I wish to quote another short paragraph from the minister's speech of October 12. On page 998 of. Hansard he is reported as having said:
It is possible to make a rough estimate only of the "savings" held by Canadian individuals in certain liquid forms.
Such an estimate, which cannot be too wide of the mark, indicates that as of May 31, 1945, in currency, bank deposits, refundable taxes and dominion government securities, Canadian individuals held savings of more than nine and a half billions and that these savings had increased by more than six and a half billions since the end of 1938. Now, sir, where did this six and a half billions come from? That is the S64 dollar question.
Another way of looking at this picture is this. In 1939 the total amount of currency in all Canada was, roughly, $200 million, and the total amount of bank deposit money was 
$2,400 million, according to the reports of the Bank of Canada. By 1945 the total amount of currency in Canada had increased to $1,070 millions, and of bank deposit money, to over $4,500 million. The supply of money in these forms has increased by $3 billion during the time when consumer goods and services were *becoming more and more scarce, and yet we have had no wild inflation. During the depression years, Mr. Dunning, then minister of finance, became quite hysterical in this house when it was suggested that $200 million of new currency be created to be put into circulation to provide jobs-get that, to provide jobs-for the unemployed and to try to check the disastrous course of deflation in this country. He said at that time, in his hysterical way, that it would be crude inflation.
But that is not all. In July, 1942, when it was suggested in this parliament that we make greater use of the Bank of Canada in conducting the war, the present Minister of Finance, as recorded at page 4271 of Hansard of 1942, stated:
If we put into circulation a billion dollars of new money, it would blow the price ceiling to kingdom come before you could say "Jack Robinson."
Now even the Minister of Finance can be wrong. When he uttered those words in this parliament in July, 1942, the total amount of public bank deposits in Canadian chartered banks, together with the total value of all notes in circulation in Canada was $3,600 million. By 1945 the aggregate of these same forms of purchasing power was $5,570,000,000. I submit that nearly twice the billion dollars of new money spoken of by my hon. friend' has been put into circulation in Canada, but I have not heard that the price ceiling has been blown to kingdom come, nor has the Minister of Finance said "Jack Robinson" so that anyone could hear him.

speechtext:
Very good. Let me make the matter perfectly clear. The type of credit expansion, the type of money that had always been recommended in the house by this group, was exactly the type of purchasing power and credit which had been used' with increasing effect during this war, exactly the same, and that is what I am referring to. Now, sir, I ask you this question: Where did' all that purchasing power come from? It was not in existence anywhere in the world in 1942. The government of Canada did not borrow it from abroad and did not create it all. I will tell hon. members where it came from. The Canadian chartered banks, who went to such pains in ithe hungry thirties to convince people that there was no money, did not differentiate between Bank of Canada notes and ordinary credit expansion. But they said that there was no money for humanitarian purposes during the months when we were suffering from unemployment and trade stagnation. During the months since 1942 the same banks have lent to various people in Canada, includ1-ing the government, nearly $2 billion of what they said they did not have, and they are receiving interest on it all.
What is the answer? I submit that the banks created and lent into circulation $2 billion of new money. They made use of the social credit of the Canadian people. They did exactly what a Social Credit government would have them do under a proper economy, except that instead of the banks being allowed to lend it into circulation, thus creating a debt to the banks on which they could continue to collect interest, the banks would
have issued money for the government interest-free and the government would have arranged for the banks a nominal service charge for services and bookkeeping.
Such a procedure would remove from the banks the power to bring on periods of deflation and their power to call in and cancel loans that had been made to the people. Many sound-money advocates entirely overlook deflation. That condition might be and often is far worse than inflation, and it has proved so in the past in Canada. Social credit money is exactly the same kind of money being used now. It is not "funny money", and I should like to emphasize that point for the benefit of hon. members who constantly shout that this is a funny money scheme. If it is, then the present situation in Canada, and the policy which has been followed since 1939, is certainly a funny money scheme. It is different from our present money-I am speaking, of course, of social credit money-but only in this respect, that it is issued into circulation without adding to the nation's debt. And remember that social creditors advocate issuing new money only when there are goods and services already in existence to be distributed by money; a dollar of purchasing power for a dollar's worth of goods and services available, no more and no less. I suggest that under such circumstances there could not possibly be any inflation.
Now let me suggest to the government that when unsaleable surpluses of goods begin to pile up on the shelves of the warehouses, as sooner or later they will because of the inherent weakness of the financial system, and when at the same time there are Canadians who need and want these goods for their own use, the government should arrange another credit expansion equal to the value of the goods to .be removed, and see to it that this new money finds its way, debt-free, into the hands of consumers, starting first with old age pensioners, the blind, scholars who want to stay in school to finish their education but have not the means to do so, and the unfortunate of the country. I suggest that no Canadian should henceforth ever have to go hungry.
I have dealt, sir, with two of the problems . which the government will doubtless encounter in its efforts to keep up the volume of production to a level which will be high enough to ensure a decent standard of living for the Canadian people to enable them to take care of the burden of taxation of their governments.
The Budget-Mr. Low

I have just one or two points to mention in conclusion, but before I sit down I should like to mention briefly a third. I shall cut it short. I refer to the problem of taxation. If we investigate carefully the conditions that existed among the Indians before the white man appeared, we shall find that the Indians were free, and they really had the spirit of freedom; there is no doubt about that. There was absence of chaos among them, and that absence of chaos was not because they did not have any government. They had a government, but the political authority that did exist in that government was devoid of the power of taxation. As we study the development of society since those very early days, we become aware of a power which gradually transformed a social government into the anti-social state. This power is the power of taxation. Many authorities, such as Jefferson of the United States and others, have warned the people that the power of taxation, placed in the hands of government, must in the end bring about a softening of the moral fibre of the people. How does that happen? The process of deterioration is quite simple. As more of the production resulting from the efforts of the individual is absorbed by the state through the ever-increasing tolls of taxation, the less the individual has for his own enjoyment, and therefore the more he has to work in order to maintain for himself circumstances that are decent in which to live.
The dignity of the individual disintegrates under the hammering of want and the fear of want. On the other hand, the power of the state increases in proportion to the wealth which it takes from tbffe people through taxation. There is an interesting aspect to this which I should like to submit to hon. members. Since wealth is economic power, then taxation simply means transferring economic power from the individual to the state. As a result of heavy taxation, and in times of depression, the individual is often pressed into Bargaining for some of what was his property by right of his own efforts in producing it. In most cases the bargaining is very much one-sided, and all too often the individual is harassed by fear and utter necessity, so that in his bargaining with the state he is forced to offer up, as the price of success, many of his rights for a simple hand-out from the government. These rights the individual has always looked upon as inalienable; but when a man is forced to seek a hand-out, whether in the form of unemployment insurance or the dole, he progressively loses his rights, and in the end he ceases to be free. This is one aspect of the taxation problem as we have experienced it down the years and since the time of the

Indians. It seems to me that we should now begin to reverse the whole process so as to revitalize and rehabilitate the individuals and to make them free.
Under the debt-financing policies followed by this and practically all other governments in democratic countries the burden of taxation of necessity grows heavier and heavier decade after decade. I have already pointed out in this house that in 1923 the people of Canada paid to the federal government 3-7/10ths per cent of the whole national income in taxes. By 1944 the taxes, to this government required 25-3/10ths per cent of the national income. To-day it requires close to 50 per cent of the total incomes of the people to meet their tax requisitions to the federal, provincial and municipal governments. It must be obvious that unless the national production is kept high, the people will not for very long be able to pay even the present high percentage of their income to the state. Yet, in their efforts to keep production up to a high level in Canada the tax structure as represented in the budget recently presented by the minister will certainly prove to be a deterrent.
I submit,.sir, that the flood-gates of production cannot be opened wide to meet the needs of Canadians unless we undertake at once a general downward division of taxation. In times of peace men will not exert themselves very hard if fully half of the product of their labour is taken from them by a super-state.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the budget debate I cannot ignore a warning recently given by an hon. member to another hon. member who, like me, was a newcomer in this chamber. Apparently one should not be obliged to wonder later on, "Was I really like that in my first session?" So, upon entering this debate in order to express a few opinions, I am filled with certain apprehensions.
I am not an expert in financial matters, and I am not one of those who consider the budget as a most fascinating adventure. The budget of a nation is filled with so many facts that in order to discuss it in all fairness, one should know all the mysteries of national and even international finance. One should also be aware of all the needs unknown to the population at large, but known by those who are in constant touch with the -pulse of the nation. I believe this is the right attitude to take in order to grasp the human element of a budget. Let us not forget that a budget is applied to- human beings and not to robots. In so far as I am concerned, this is the angle in which I am interested.
If the statement handed down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) gives us a general picture, often without details as to the origin of particular needs of various parts of the country, it dbes not mean that in order to obtain a final result local questions had to be ignored, and that the country had to be considered as an indivisible entity. I would believe rather that particular attention was paid to the various needs created by the geographical position, local production and particularly the human condition, of the many classes which constitute the Canadian nation,
Representing one of these districts that has special needs which are sometimes common to the whole country, I believe it is my duty to speak in the name of the county where was bom and where studied Sir Whlfrid Laurier. During the war an attempt was made to give mankind a superhuman stature;
from the physical point of view the maximum had to be exceeded, and morally our minds had to be directed exclusively toward one goal. It was most extraordinary that we succeeded and that- this success has lasted for six years. The torch race was kept, up at the same speed unceasingly without the runner ever falling. Now the race is over, but how is the runner?
In order to form a true picture there is nothing like looking around. Near the town of Joliette in my riding the largest war factory in Canada, and even, as I am told, in the empire, was established. Where wealthy farmers lived thirteen- thousand people came and through their work supported the armies of the united nations. From the St. Lawrence in the south to the Laurential forests in the north; that is, from the factories to the lumber camps, everything was directed toward the war effort.
Grappling with a thousand problems, agriculture was endeavouring to obtain manpower from the factories. Organized labour, constantly growing stronger in centres like Joliette close to Montreal, threatened to spread even to the smallest districts. And now? War factories are slowing down their production and forcing workers back to their original homes. Our veterans are coming back from overseas. Lumber camps are asking for workers whom sometimes they cannot find. Agriculture, with a greatly increased production, is also suffering from a lack of manpower. In the industrial field the smaller industries view with anxiety the excessive expansion of large manufacturing industries.
The enthusiasm shown, during the last war loan reveals nevertheless that the Canadian people are confident in their lucky star and are ready to face the problems of the future. By no means are. they exhausted by the hardships of war. Now all this must be directed toward a peace effort as sustained as was our war effort. It is in these circumstances that the population of my county were expecting the budget speech, and I believe the5r repeat the words which the financial critic of the opposition said in the house immediately after the budget. He said, "The minister has removed from the minds of the people of Canada a fear which many of them had." It is true the same critic said shortly afterwards, "Has the government really developed a peace-time mentality in the question of public finance?" This worry was rather peculiar since the hon. member seemed to ignore the significant words of the Minister of Finance.
The minister stated that war expenditures never decrease as quickly as war undertakings. That is true. When shells cease being fired on
The Budget-Mr. Lapalme

the battlefield the home front does not collapse suddenly. The nation's economy cannot revert overnight to its pre-war position. Therefore .the budget speech, in the words of the opposition, has removed a fear which many people had.
I wrould not be truly representing a county which is the centre of tobacco growing in the province of Quebec if I did not direct attention to the following statement made by the Minister of Finance:
We foresee an increase in the revenue from excise taxes and duties on tobacco.
As far as I can remember, Joliette in the province of Quebec has always b,een the-most important market for raw leaf tobacco for pipe use. Furthermore, in the last few years Joliette has become the only place in Quebec where Quebec cigarette tobacco is both produced and graded. It is quite normal, as was stated in the budget speech, to expect increased revenues from this source. However, I should like to make a few comments which may not be a warning but which will recall certain facts that are capable of leading to serious thinking.
An increase in production and sales of cigarettes and raw leaf tobacco in Ontario and Quebec will certainly bring about an increase in excise revenue. The Ontario marketing board in setting a price of 331 cents a pound for cigarette tobacco has had an effect upon the 4,500,000 pounds produced in the Joliette district. This increases prices to a higher level than during previous years. This is of interest, not only to the growers but to the department of revenue. As far as cigarette tobacco is concerned, if I had a cause to defend I would defend that of the growers because this trade is exclusively in the hands of the larger industries which are not to be pitied.
But the same situation does not exist with raw leaf tobacco for pipe use or even for cigars. In this field, both the farmer and the trading manufacturer, if not the cooperative as well, have a worthy cause. Formerly-and here I am recalling personal recollections, because for family and local reasons I have spent all my life among tobacco even though I am a lawyer actually-the trade in raw leaf tobacco in the Joliette district was divided among many trading manufacturers of various importance who each hired a certain number of workers who earned an honourable living out of this business. This was a small industry, humble but alive. Purchasing and selling were a very simple matter. I remember as distinctly as if it were yesterday seeing transactions between grower and dealer performed without any written document on the running board of a car or in a buggy.

,Everyone knows what changes were brought about by the war of 191448. Taxation, like other things, became of full age. The raw leaf tobacco grown in Canada was affected, but only for a short time. Conditions became normal but afterward deteriorated in a sensational manner. At the present time the tax is twenty-eight cents a pound. I cannot tell if contraband is at the same rate as this tax, because here as elsewhere we have "free traders."
A certain difference in price has always existed between Quebec and Ontario tobaccos; prices for Quebec tobaccos have always been higher because of the varieties that are grown. What was bound to happen has happened. As far back as 1918-19 dealers in Kent and Essex counties began to build up an export business from Ontario to Quebec, which business persisted until it was stopped a few days ago by a federal order. Therefore in our district we are acquainted with the Ontario tobacco market, especially since we now grow cigarette tobacco on a large scale.
As was often asked, was the infiltration in retail trade of Ontario tobacco branded with a Quebec label a factor in creating the truly rotten situation which exists at present? I leave the answer to specialists. Nevertheless, in this matter, nothing can be compared with the tax which, according to fluctuations in prices, always amounts in normal times to at least twice the purchasing price; occasionally it is even four times this price.
Furthermore, the prices and trade board, for many months if not years during this war, set the sales price of dealers at a lower level than the price paid growers. While I was preparing these notes, dealers learned that a new order was upsetting the market for small tobaccos. I believe that it could have been possible to do justice to all without running the risk of ruining those who, after all, maintained this business during many years. When the last order setting prices of the present crop was passed, the dealers had bought all the small tobaccos at a higher price than that which they should have paid in order to sell this tobacco -in accordance with the rates established in this order, which by that very fact had a retroactive effect.
Here we have an industry which formerly was prosperous, which supplied work in many small centres throughout the province and, all things, considered, even handled a large volume of business. To-day, it is no more what it used to be. To-morrow, will it have completely vanished? It is said that trusts are threatening it; would this be true? Will cooperatives be successful in saving it? I hope so; nevertheless I ask the government

The Budget-Mr. Lapalme
to think the matter over twice before they allow this industry to die. It is worth the trouble of lightening the leaden cloak which is smothering it, and which is called taxation.
I know very well that first of all we must reduce taxes on the necessities of life, and that tobacco cannot be placed in that category. But what permits us to obtain these necessities? At any rate, as soon as circumstances permit, it is to be hoped that government officials will review this situation, and by doing so they would only be doing justice to this cause. I have just used a great word- "justice". Indeed it recalls the claims of all nations, and especially, with an ever more disquieting acuteness, the claims of labour. Moreover, all social classes are demanding it.
At this moment, I am reminded that, in the economic history of our times, if labour, and especially organized labour, were often ostracized by employers, it would be dangerous for the opposite reaction to occur nowadays. Revolutions always were reactions of this kind. Two factors, usually determine the swing of the pendulum: the human factor and the economic factor; we are dealing with men, and men are prompted by needs.
These thoughts are going through my mind because I am aware that the budget shows the ever-increasing importance which the Department of Labour assumes in public expenditures. Labour is part of the social problem. I said, "part" of the social problem. It does not by itself constitute the whole social problem, though it takes much space in the picture we have of the world. The social problem affects everyone; labour is one of its most important elements. It is worthy of all our attention.
In a discussion of the budget, it is very difficult to restrict to figures this complex question. It is quite true that one can always mention with satisfaction the lowering of income tax with respect to the working classes, together with a thought for agriculture when one considers the tax exemption on machinery used for producing food.
But the labour problem takes on an altogether different meaning when it is connected to man himself man who is made [DOT] of intelligence and flesh. It is the family question, the dwelling conditions, the conditions of his labour, his security, his health, his immediate and remote future.
Family allowances have become part of his social life. Why not his house; why not tomorrow the family salary? Talking of his house, undoubtedly one thinks of the labourer living in a large city. I am thinking especially of small towns like mine. The town of Joliette has a population of approximately 15,000
people. The surrounding population raises this figure to 18,000. What does the National Housing Act do for them? Nothing; we are ignored. It is all the more impossible to obtain help in a small village. Joliette had her glorious dead on the battlefront; a few hundred veterans of the three armed services are coming back. Will they be able to rely on Wartime Housing? I hope so, but I am doubtful. In the meantime, those who intend to build must rely on their own means only.
It has been said of the labourer: "Give him a fair salary and everything will be all right." A fair and reasonable salary is necessary, but the increase in salaries will reach its ceiling some day, and one cannot expect an indefinite progression toward astronomical figures. This state of uncertainty must cease.
What then, is more stable than a home and a house? In a travesty of what I was saying a while ago respecting salaries, one could say: "Give the labourer his own house, and everything will be quiet and stable." If I speak in this manner, it is because I consider the labourer as a man, and too many laws have disregarded man. Instinctively and out of necessity, is it not true that man will look for a shelter before he will even look for a living? Social peace will find therein one of its' main props, because this problem, as a member stated in the house, is truly a social as well as an economic problem. As long as we are at the mercy of financial organizations in connection with cheap dwellings in smaller centres, I am sure of this: In their eyes, we will remain of no importance. Until to-day, they have done nothing for us.
During the last six years, the country has lent billions to the government ; now in return, could the government not lend1 directly to the people? Is this impossible? Farm loans were carried into effect; direct loans for the .purpose of erecting houses to be occupied by their owners could also be carried out. This is not in contradiction of my request for lowering taxes on tobacco-because I am advocating a loan, not a gift. A special organization could thus work toward improving the social standard, as directly and as effectively as family allowances.
I wish to request for the benefit of labour the help of the financial organization called the industrial development bank, and I make this request seriously. If this bank cannot be of any benefit to smaller industries in all our provinces, then local labour will be the loser. Until now, this bank has not yet revealed1 its existence in my county, which is one of the most thickly populated rural constituencies in the country.
The Budget

Mr. Lapalme

It is quite true that all these social problems may assume more importance in the succeeding budgets after an agreement has been reached over federal-provincial matters, and we may entertain the hope of a complete agreement. I am quite in favour of provincial autonomy, but I am more strongly in favour of the welfare of the total Canadian population. To help labour, give it homes; grant it monthly allowances. Among other things, these are means which are capable of giving to the nation a robust health and a stable economy. As it was written recently: "Economy, instead of serving the golden gods, will serve mankind."
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, pre-war budgets can no longer be expected. We can no longer ignore the social needs which war has so bluntly revealed. We shall soon be confronted with the problem of finding employment for all. And then, going outside our own boundaries, we shall participate in the reorganization of a world with which we are bound up.
At the very moment when the, nation's demands on the government are heaviest, the Minister of Finance will be asked to reduce the taxes. A heavy task is thus devolved upon this generation, and especially upon those who have to manage the national economy.
My preceding remarks were intended to be helpful and constructive. This budget comes during the transition period and it already gives us a welcome reminder of the restoration of peace. Let us hope that the next one will take us outside the realm of war so that we- may attend still more earnestly to the solution of our social problems..
In concluding, I wish to bring to.'the attention of the government a matter which is of special concern to my -constituency.
The plant at St. Paul 1'Ermite to which I referred at the beginning of my remarks has cost about twenty million dollars, I believe. A short time before the- end of the war, we were promised that it would be kept in operation even after the cessation of hostilities. Nevertheless, it is no longer ini operation. Am I going too far in recalling those former promises?
(Text): Mr. Speaker, at this moment when ' victory is still in our memories-and may we never forget it!-when the country has just shown in a resounding way its faith in peace to the same extent that it has done in war, I believe that social questions have become the most important issues of the moment. Canada has already begun to lead the way in this field; in thus continuing, it may probably find what it needs above all-national unity.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is only one way in which we can judge the present budget: Do its proposals give the assurance that the government is taking its full employment policies seriously? Thjs is the first peace-time budget since 1939 and was brought down at a time when the country is faced with the problems of reconversion from war to peace, lay-offs and the need to maintain consumer purchasing power. The people are looking to the budget for an indication of the plans of the government to maintain employment, to provide jobs for the workers and for the men and women who are returning from overseas. People want to see whether this budget provides for the social security measures that are necessary, and for large scale housing and for other measures that will make it possible to avoid an early post-war depression. It is against the background of this urgency that we should examine the budget before the house.
It is most appropriate to remind the house of some of the government's -own statements of policy and of what it thinks is the actual job of a budget. In its white paper, "Employment and Income," issued last April, the government stated:
Fiscal policy during_ the war has necessarily been based on economic as much as purely financial considerations. It is proposed to extend that practice into the post-war years and apply war experience to the problems of peace.
In the same white paper we further read:
The government will be prepared in periods when unemployment threatens to incur -the deficits and increases in the national debt resulting from its employment and income policy.
In the proposals of the federal government to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction we find this statement:
It is the responsibility of the government to pursue policies that create conditions in which the initiative, energy and resourcefulness of individual citizens can .achieve rising standards of life. The modern governmental budget must he the balance wheel of the economy.
With this, Mr. Speaker, I fully agree. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) elaborated on this subject in introducing his budget to the house, when, he said:
The government has adopted as a major aim of government policy the maintenance of a high and stable level of income and employment. Accordingly it has become a major consideration in budget policy.
But when we look at the budget and its application we find none of the promises of the white paper fulfilled and none of the things contained in the proposals of the dominion government to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction, nor do we find any substantiation of the statement made by

The Budget-Mr. Rose
the Minister of Finance to the house. This budget does not help to maintain full employment; it does not provide for it, and therefore we find that government practice is quite out of line with government theory.
How are those job to be provided? On the basis of this budget the jobs are to be provided by holding out to big business so-called incentives. If incentives are necessary, it is the Canadian people who need them because 'big business which talks so much of the need for incentives in order to give more employment has already had enough incentives given it to provide full employment for the people of Canada. For instance, the Bank of Canada statistical summary, analysing the account of 700 Canadian companies, points out that after taxes and depreciation the net income to the stockholders increased from $242 million in 1938 to $292 million in 1943. The increase in profits before taxes was of course much greater. Profits increased from $410 million in 1938 to $799 million in 1943. But there is much more to the picture than that. Accumulated surpluses and surplus reserves increased from $800 million in 1938 to $1,188 million in 1943; and at the same time these companies were able to reduce their funded debt from $1,015 million to $892 million.
Individuals as well as corporations have not done badly for themselves during the war years. In 1937-38, according to figures given by the Minister of Finance to the house on March 24, 1939, as reported in Hansard, there were 382 Canadians at that time receiving incomes of more than $50,000 a year. In 1944, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, there were 650 persons in the same income bracket, receiving a total income of $68 million, or better than $100,000 apiece. After taxes, they still had a trifle of $25 million left. That is not too bad for only 650 people. The minister in his budget now proposes to give these people $95 million more through the proposed reduction in the excess profits tax. My party, the Labour Progressive party, has stated in its programme that the excess profits tax after the war should continue as in war time and should be used for the community as a whole; that is, for a redistribution of income. The present budget does not provide for a redistribution of income, because if it gives anything it gives it to the rich. It makes some concessions to smaller business, and with this I fully agree. That is, small business with profits of less than $25,000 gets some concessions. That is good. But as regards the vast majority of Canadians the budget proposals do not assist in building up their purchasing power. There
was quite a bit of pressure from big business for concessions, and concessions were granted. But the people of Canada-and I am thinking especially or organized labour-have been making certain demands. Through their trades unions the labour movement called for tax exemptions to be raised to $2,400 for married persons and $1,000 for single persons. Their voice was not heeded. Instead, the budget provides for a straight sixteen per cent reduction in personal income tax. This gives very little additional money to the majority of the people but provides a substantial roll to the higher income groups.
The figures I am about to cite are revealing in this respect. They were worked out on the basis of information from the dominion bureau of statistics. They show the following: a group with an income of over $25,000, and numbering about 2,900, will benefit by $15 million. That is, 2,900 people who have each ah income of more than $25,000 will get, as a result of this sixteen per cent reduction, an aggregate of $15 million, or $5,000 apiece. Not bad. But what happens to the mass of taxpayers, those-and there are 1,675,000 of them -whose incomes are less than $2,000 each? The total tax reduction will give them $26,600,000, or $15.90 apiece. There is quite a difference there.
Here are a few more figures in this connection. Those with incomes under $1,000 number sixteen percent of the taxpayers, but they get less than three per cent of the, total tax reduction. Those, however, with incomes of over $25,000, number only one-tenth of one per cent of the taxpayers; yet they get 13Jj per cent of the total tax reduction. These figures reveal quite a contrast between the government's treatment of the wealthy taxpayer and of the man' in the street. There are many more concessions in the budget to men of means. There is the repeal of the ten per cent war exchange tax on goods imported from outside the British empire. The eight per cent tax on machinery is repealed. But will .these concessions be passed on to the consumer? No, they will not. This will only mean more profits and more accumulations for those who already have plenty.
I oppose the reduction in the excess profits tax, as well as the minister's proposals for the sixteen per cent reduction; that is, the straight sixteen per cent reduction in personal income tax. Because the budget fails to put money into the pockets of the people who need it, I cannot support this budget.
Further, the budget does not provide for the health and well-being of the Canadian people. While on that topic I wish to mention a manifesto which, no doubt in common with
The Budget-Mr. Rose

many other hon. members, I received the other day from the Canadian Legion. This document points out that Canada has still to achieve the ideals of peace, and one of those ideals, according to the legion manifesto, is decent homes for Canadians. I quote the following passage: . '
Hundreds of thousands of houses will need to be built. Yet homes are more than houses, and Canadians have the challenging task of creating the kind of homes and family life that will make this nation strong, clean, united.
The budget before the house has not been worked out in that spirit. It provides neither for houses nor for the families who would live in those houses. Service men and service women are returning home only to find that there are no homes for them. They saved Canada, they helped to save the world, but they are unable to find decent homes in which to start life anew with their wives and children. It is estimated that 43 per cent of the returned men have no proper housing.
But the plight of returned men only reflects the plight of many other Canadians regarding houses, a situation which was aggravated by the war. In 1946 Canada will be short of 500,000 houses, excluding rural needs. The houses of 350,000 Canadians are sub-standard. Of a total of 2,635,753 houses in Canada, approximately 600,000 are obsolete. One-third of all Canadians live in bad and overcrowded houses because they cannot afford good hous-. ing; they can afford to pay only between $10 and $20 a month in rent, and even with the aid of family allowances they can pay no more without injuring the health of their families by cutting down on food. Lack of housing and bad housing take a terrific toll of the people.
Sociologists who have made a study of the effects of present conditions on the people have the following to say with respect to United States citizens:
Of the slums and blighted districts comprising about 20 per cent of the metropolitan residential areas they account for 33 per cent of the population, 45 per cent of the major crimes, 55 per cent of child delinquency, 60 per cent of tuberculosis victims, and 45 per cent of city city service costs.
On a number of occasions I have mentioned in this house similar effects on the people in our own country and have pointed to conditions in Montreal. In 1941 it was estimated that the city of Montreal needed 50,000 dwellings. How many were built? In 1944 there were 2,618 units, and in 1945 there were 2,241 units. At this rate it will take twenty years to make up the backlog without allowing for increasing requirements in the years ahead. By the end of this year 5,000 homes will be
fMr. Rose.]
needed by returning men. To add to the seriousness of the situation in Montreal, of the homes put up in 1944 and 1945, 90 per cent are rented at over $40 a month. This lets out 76 per cent of the population whose income does not permit them to rent houses at' such high figures.
The other day the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) said, in regard to housing, t-hat every member-not just one but everyone of us-knows that the housing situation to-day is one of the most serious conditions in Canada. That is true and we all agree with that statement. But iwhat are we going to do about this situation? It is not enough to agree that it is bad. We have legislation and present legislation has not provided houses. Nine out of every ten houses built at the present time are being built outside this legislation, and even those built under this legislation are not within the reach of the worker or of the veteran who is not sure about the future. It should be established once and for all that it is not profitable for the private builder to construct low-rental houses, and he definitely will mot do it for love. This has been the experience in every country and also in Canada. In war time, when we needed tanks, guns, aeroplanes, munitions, the government cut the red tape and saw to it that these materials were produced. Huge munitions plants were built in a few months. There was a feeling of urgency. Well, there is similar urgency at the present time in the matter of housing, and the government must act in a manner different from that which has characterized it up to the present moment. The building of houses will also provide jobs.
How is the government going to deal with this housing problem? The Labour Progressive party proposes that $1 billion, raised through a loan, be used by the government to build 250,000 housing units in the period of five years. I would say that such a slogan as "Buy a bond to build a home for a Canadian" would receive the necessary response from all Canadians, and such bouses should be assigned to the communities that need them and to the people requiring houses, on a basis of priority: No. 1, veterans; No. 2, slum dwellers; No. 3, people who require extra living space.
That is the way in which this will have to be done. I know there are constitutional problems, but the government must find ways and means of building these homes, constitutional problems notwithstanding. Britain has built 1,250,000 low-rent houses-how? The government lends construction capital to the municipal housing board and pays a rent subsidy. Private contractors build the houses-

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
That is the answer for Canada. That is also the answer to the problem of jobs. The construction industry estimates that $500 million a year on construction would provide 479,000 men with jobs. That is the answer.
There can be no piecemeal measures about this, because such measures will not solve the problem. The government must change its attitude toward the problem. I understand that to-day the British government has announced a housing programme which is altogether different from anything that has gone before. They realize that .there is an emergency and are acting accordingly. We in Canada must act from a similar spirit. It is true that our houses were not bombed, but we harm plenty of slums and we need houses. We raised $18 billions for war. Surely we can raise SI billion for homes.
A few weeks ago we concluded the ninth victory loan. The slogan was "Sign your name to victory". I would say that the government will not be signing its name to victory unless it provides for homes and for the welfare of the Canadian people.
